Such results are essential for transferring theorems from commutative algebra between characteristic-zero and positive-characteristic contexts. We offer multiple applications, including a novel proof of the inductive step in the nullstellensatz over Z, and a simplified demonstration that for ideals in k[x1,...,xn] with a specified sub-linear complexity bound, the dimension and reducibility of the variety are determined by the generic dimension and reducibility, respectively. Additionally, we present an alternative proof (without a specific complexity bound) that a variety is irreducible if and only its coordinate ring is integrally closed. These findings also yield an alternative characterization of reducibility via the existence of zero-divisors. Furthermore, we establish the equivalence between the non-singularity of a variety and its coordinate ring, and show that irreducible varieties are non-singular at all but a closed set of lower dimension. Finally, we prove the existence of an algorithm to decide the complexity-bound reducibility of an ideal. The primary innovation of this paper lies in utilizing a straightforward complexity bound to establish the equivalence of Reducibility0 and the family of Reducivityp structures, thereby enabling the application of Deformation Theory to translate positive-characteristic results to characteristic zero, a theory previously employed to prove the above theorems. This approach contrasts with traditional methods that rely on more complex structures like Hilbert schemes or Groebner bases, which are not suitable for this characterization. A defining feature of this Deformation Theory is its reliance on a single, unified mathematical object that connects the variety and its reductions, rather than distinct structures for each prime. This object, termed a Local Semi-Parametric Lifting, was not considered in prior literature, as existing approaches lacked a global object capable of linking all local positive-characteristic analyses to the original variety. Additionally, this method avoids the need for the theorem statements to explicitly reference a specific complexity bound. The key technical components are the definitions of reducibility and non-singularity as first-order properties, the use of Chevalley's Theorem, and the application of the EGA Pseudo-Valuation Criterion for reducibility and non-singularity.

We provide a complete characterization of this functor's image, demonstrating that it yields a subcategory of $k$-fold vector bundles comprising symmetric structures equipped with a family of morphisms indexed by the symmetric group ${\mathbb S}_k$. Notably, in the degree 2 case, this added structure defines a symplectical double vector bundle, representing the skew-symmetric counterpart to a metric double vector bundle. Furthermore, we examine the related scenario of fully linearising $N$-manifolds and illustrate how the full linearisation functor enables the "superisation" of a graded bundle. These results have significant applications in the classification of graded bundles and $N$-manifolds, as well as in the study of fully linearised structures on these objects. Entirely independent, this work also offers a constructive method to fully linearise graded bundles when the first jet extension is available. Additionally, the findings are relevant for fully linearising a graded metric of degree 1 and for achieving superisation within the category of supermanifolds. Former research has primarily focused on first-order properties, such as trivialisation via flat connections, jet extensions, and their counterparts involving superisations. In contrast, this work addresses the complete description of linearisation at an arbitrary point. Beyond standard data like the tangent space and its iterated tangent spaces, the tangent space of a graded manifold includes the cotangent space and its duals, along with specific morphisms between them. In the context of a manifold with structure, such as a graded bundle, these components can be derived from the tangent fibre. However, reconstructing the full tangent space from the tangent fibre is generally complex and, to the authors' knowledge, has not been previously solved for the specific case of ${\mathbb Z}_k$-manifolds. Although intricate, this reconstruction is made possible by the structure of jet extensions in a way that mirrors the straightforward procedure found in the $\mathbb Z_2$-case. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the necessary background on graded manifolds, emphasizing their equivalence with graded bundles of degree 1, and introduces the concept of a $\mathbb N_k$-manifold. Although scattered light inherently contains both the amplitude and phase of the electromagnetic field, phase data is frequently discarded during standard intensity measurements. Nevertheless, phase information is often critical for reconstructing target details, a principle established in coherent x-ray imaging. This work presents a novel phase retrieval algorithm capable of recovering field phase data from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra. We demonstrate this technique using x-ray scattering at the iXS beamline at MAX IV Laboratory. Employing a well-known x-ray technique, we phase retrieve data from an x-ray laser experiment featuring two x-ray pulses with energies above and below the iodine core-level threshold. Furthermore, we show that this approach enables a novel analysis method for x-ray Raman spectra from a molecular gas target. Through a quantitative comparison of retrieved phases between an experimental result derived from a simplified theoretical model and a reference value, we confirm that our method successfully preserves phase data. Furthermore, the phase values align with expectations from an established quantitative analysis technique, indicating that this approach can recover phase information even from x-ray beams with relatively low brightness. Consequently, this method is anticipated to be widely applicable to various experimental setups, including those involving dark beam data from the proposed iXM at MAX IV. Finally, the technique can be readily adapted to other facilities possessing similar capabilities.

We derive the hybrid-mixed formulation for the stability analysis of the corresponding imaginary wavenumber modes and demonstrate that this approach is equivalent to the standard pressure-based finite element method for purely oscillatory modes. However, we identify that, unlike the standard method, the hybrid-mixed formulation eliminates zero wavenumber numerical instability. Using a W1 element for the velocity field, we determine that all non-zero mode frequencies are unstable, save for a specific subset of wavenumbers when the viscosity is extremely low. For a given mass, these unstable modes share a comparable maximum magnitude. We also compare our findings with results obtained from an explicit integration scheme. This study provides a robust numerical framework for investigating complex hydrodynamical problems involving viscous fluids.

Although Bayes factors provide a direct approach to hypothesis evaluation, they are notably sensitive to specific data characteristics and model assumptions. Furthermore, their practical implementation remains uncertain regarding its robustness to computational details. This study examines these issues within the context of cognitive science applications. We clarify the statistical foundations of Bayes factors for Bayesian inference and emphasize the necessity of utility functions for making principled decisions. Additionally, we investigate the behavior of Bayes factors under various conditions, including errors in estimation. Notably, it remains unclear whether bridge sampling yields unbiased estimates for complex analyses; we address this by employing simulation-based calibration for the first time to assess the accuracy of such estimates. Our analysis also covers the stability of Bayes factors across different MCMC samples, their dependence on data variations, and the variability of resulting decisions, proposing methods to optimize these decisions via utility functions. We outline a reproducible workflow for researchers to test the robustness of Bayes factors in their specific analyses, illustrated with a case study from cognitive science. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a framework for evaluating the strengths and limitations of Bayes factors as a metric for scientific evidence. Reproducible code is accessible at https://osf.io/y354c/.

By applying the Burer-Monteiro factorization within a specific Riemannian quotient geometry, we analyze the resulting unconstrained low-dimensional optimization landscape. While the factorized objective is generally non-convex, we demonstrate that every critical point is also convex relative to the original high-dimensional objective. This confirms the success of the Burer-Monteiro approach when the objective rank is fixed. Additionally, if the objective rank exceeds the objective dimension, the landscape becomes globally convex. These findings align with and extend previous research, offering new insights for objective ranks where the dimension exceeds the rank. Furthermore, our proofs provide a fresh perspective on global convexity for well-known problems like weighted graph PCA. Crucially, unlike earlier works that relied on the Kurdyka-Łojasiewicz (KL) inequality, our proof does not require the objective dimension to be odd, thereby generalizing the global convexity of PCA's Burer-Monteiro landscape beyond the case where the dimension is two times plus one. Overall, these results underscore the landscape's favorable properties and suggest that efficient local methods, such as gradient descent, can solve high-dimensional PCA with objective rank R = 2 without needing an initialization closer to a global minimizer than $O(1/\sqrt{n})$. We extend these conclusions to a non-differentiable regularized landscape. Extensive numerical experiments further validate these theoretical findings. Our contributions advance the landscape analysis of PCA and related problems, particularly by establishing global convexity and identifying the exact threshold for this property. These results also strengthen earlier evidence that the Burer-Monteiro factorization yields a simple objective free from spurious local minima for finite sum objectives with objective rank equal to the data dimension.

Our introduced "social-learning" variants successfully establish this equilibrium, whereas "individual learning" versions fail to converge strategies to the Nash outcome. When players utilize "canonical co-evolutionary genetic algorithms," the game dynamics form an ergodic Markov Chain; consequently, we analyze simulation results using both specific methodologies and broader statistical tests. These analyses reveal that in the "social" scenario, states corresponding to Nash Equilibrium play are highly frequent within the chain's stationary distribution, while in the "individual learning" scenario, they are exceedingly rare. Furthermore, the time required for "social learning" players to reach the Nash Equilibrium is significantly shorter than the lifespan of the Markov Chain's transient states. In contrast, "individual learning" players never attain the Nash Equilibrium. The "social" approach appears to facilitate reachability because it prevents the genetic algorithm from wasting evaluations on long-term suboptimal solutions that lack a direct path to long-run optimality. Specifically, players can episodically exploit a Nash Equilibrium once found without incurring a large fitness penalty, as the Nash equilibrium represents a state of stability. Additionally, a small population size is not a limiting factor; a population of 20 is sufficient to reach the equilibrium within a reasonable timeframe. This study offers insights valuable for understanding human decision-making processes and has significant relevance to regulatory bodies and anti-trust agencies.

Extending beyond simple word alignment, we implement multiple cluster-level alignments, ensuring that word clusters maintain consistent distributions across different languages. Our clustering strategy leverages three distinct signals: (1) neighboring words within monolingual embedding spaces, (2) character-level data, and (3) linguistic properties (such as apposition and locative suffixes) extracted from linguistic structure knowledge bases supporting thousands of languages. Abstract: This study introduces a cross-lingual name tagging framework for Wikipedia based on distributed representation learning. Unlike prior work focusing solely on language identification, our framework accounts for cross-lingual entity alignment, leveraging three types of cluster-consistent embeddings: one based on contextual information and two based linguistic structure knowledge. We validate the model's effectiveness through intrinsic evaluations on multilingual QVEC tasks and an extrinsic evaluation on a real-world Wikipedia name tagging dataset. Our results show significant improvements, an 11% increase in F-score compared to previous studies. Additionally, we assess the framework's utility on low-resource languages and confirm its efficacy by reconstructing entity links in a multilingual Wikipedia database. The framework is accessible at https://github.com/AlirezaShamshiri/COL-NT-Wiki.

Transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) spectra and integrated yields are derived across various centrality bins, ranging from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb collisions, characterized by final-state multiplicity. By examining both Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions, the study investigates systems with comparable charged-particle multiplicities but distinct initial geometrical eccentricities. A detailed comparison of spectral shapes between these two systems highlights an inverse relationship between radial and elliptic flow. Specifically, the results indicate that radial flow remains independent of the colliding system when normalized to similar charged-particle multiplicities. Regarding hadron chemistry, the previously noted smooth progression of particle ratios with multiplicity from small to large systems is also observed in Xe-Xe collisions. Furthermore, these findings confirm that two key characteristics of particle production at LHC energies apply to medium-sized nuclei: a proton-to-pion ratio lower than thermal model predictions and an increasing $\phi$-to-pion ratio as final-state multiplicity rises. Finally, the data support the hypothesis that the thermal density parameter $a$ in the Hadron Resonance Gas model is not a function of the colliding system's size, nor does it exhibit a trend with entropy per unit rapidity in heavy-ion collisions. On the aspect of collective flow, a constituent quark scaling pattern with $p_{\rm T}$ persists across medium-baryon density ($\beta_s$) in Xe-Xe collisions. Additionally, the ratio of elliptic to radial flow is also linked to the quark number scaling. Collectively, these results indicate that phenomena previously established in LHC heavy-ion collisions are present at even higher energies and affect medium-sized nuclei.

9, Chile, particularly its capital Santiago, experienced extensive violence that resulted in the destruction of both public and private infrastructure. This study seeks to extend an epidemiological non-local model, previously effective in describing the 2005 French riots, to include the topological structure of Santiago's subway network and account for the observed spatial distribution of rioting. While the model accurately replicated the aggregated temporal progression of the disorders, it failed to reproduce the actual spatial pattern of activity in Santiago. This discrepancy is primarily due to the model's absence of a population displacement mechanism, a factor deemed essential for explaining the unrest episodes in the city. Although incorporating such advection-type dynamics remains inherently difficult, a simplified approach was employed to demonstrate its capacity to replicate the observed spatial distribution of violence. These findings underscore the necessity of integrating key behavioral aspects, such as population movement, into mathematical frameworks to achieve a comprehensive understanding and effective management of urban riots. The proposed framework may also prove applicable to other large-scale collective phenomena, including urban traffic flow, disaster response following events like earthquakes, and the propagation of rumors or viral content on social media.

Unlike standard methods that fail to address extended operators or infinite alphabets, the proposed algorithm bypasses the conversion to equivalent automata. Instead, it employs a purely symbolic term rewriting system to resolve regular expression inequalities. The authors present a new symbolic decision procedure for containment, utilizing Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives alongside Antimirov's rewriting technique. Furthermore, they extend Brzozowski's syntactic derivative operator into two generalized versions capable of operating on representable, potentially infinite character sets. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method is highly effective, often outperforming state-of-the-art solutions by several orders of magnitude. Regular expressions are fundamental across various fields, including program analysis, compiler development, and library creation; however, determining the containment of one expression within another is computationally challenging. The paper's proposed technique is particularly valuable because it is non-standard, avoiding the typically expensive transformation of expressions into equivalent automata. Additionally, the algorithm exhibits robustness when handling large expression sizes. Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives, originally devised for minimization, are shown to be extremely powerful when combined with Antimirov's rewriting. This finding contributes a reliable and efficient algorithm to the field of logic and computation. Furthermore, the technique is broadly applicable to any domain involving symbol manipulation, such as proving equivalences or establishing ordering between abstract syntax trees in programming languages like Haskell, Python, or C++. . Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) leverages data from cameras and inertial sensors to determine position and orientation. Recently, deep learning-based VIO approaches have gained significant interest because they derive pose information through data-driven methods, eliminating the need for manually designed algorithms. However, current learning-based VIO systems typically depend on recurrent models to integrate multimodal data and process sensor signals, which often struggle with training difficulties and lack sufficient efficiency. We introduce a novel learning-based VIO framework utilizing external memory attention, which effectively and efficiently fuses visual and inertial features for state estimation. This proposed model achieves accurate and robust pose estimation, even in challenging conditions such as overcast days and water-covered terrain—scenarios where traditional VIO algorithms fail to extract visual features. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses both conventional and existing learning-based VIO baselines across various scenes, with further validation provided by ablation studies. Additionally, comparative analysis of our method against alternative models highlights the network's efficiency in handling data fusion. The source code for our framework is accessible at: \url{https://github.com/yiyiyi0322/MEMA-VIO}.

This Letter introduces a square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal (SHOWS) model by adapting characteristics from its parent Hamiltonians. Our findings reveal that SHOWS supports both "Fermi-arc" surface states and hinge states linking the projections of Weyl points. We successfully constructed this exotic SHOWS state theoretically and observed it experimentally in three-dimensional (3D) stacked electric circuits featuring honeycomb-kagome hybridizations and double-helix interlayer couplings. These results pave the way for achieving square-root topology within 3D solid-state systems. The concept of square-root topology, initially prominent in 2D photonic and electromagnetic systems, has received limited attention in 3D solid-state physics. We define a material as SHOWS when its Fermi surfaces consist of arc-like structures originating from higher-order Weyl points (HWP SHOWS) or hinge states (hinge SHOWS). While our realization targets 3D square-root semimetal states, the design principles applicable to SHOWS also offer a pathway to square-root Weyl semimetals (SWSMs), which possess Fermi surfaces corresponding to HWPs or hinge SHOWS. This comparison of SHOWS and SWSM provides a foundational framework for exploring cubic-root topology in future research. SHOWS represents a novel material class featuring honeycomb-kagome structures, distinguishing it from existing photonic and mechanical systems. Furthermore, our work demonstrates that complex, experimentally viable exotic square-root topological phases can be achieved by strategically combining known semimetal states.

To better understand the quantum thermodynamics of many-body systems, we investigate whether the QNEC constrains irreversible entropy production during quenches driven by energy-momentum inflow from an infinite bath. Our results indicate that while the QNEC provides only a loose bound for quenches involving infinite baths in one and two dimensions, it is optimized by the models most relevant to quantum criticality—specifically, the massless Dirac fermion and Tomonaga-Luttinger models in one dimension. We further extend this analysis to one-dimensional systems interacting within the Tolman temperature gradient of a uniform acceleration field. Our findings demonstrate that the QNEC becomes a tight bound in this context for the Tomonaga-Luttinger model across all interaction strengths, but for the many-body Dirac model only, which lacks scattering and thus entails no irreversibility. Collectively, these results suggest that nature may prefer the most efficient bound on entropy production when defining parameters along interactionless trajectories in the coupling space. Additionally, we offer an analogy linking the QNEC to the second law of thermodynamics and an additional bound on irreversible entropy production derived from the strong subadditivity of entanglement entropy. To support our claims, we work with two one-dimensional models solvable under uniform acceleration: the Massless Dirac model under a thermal bath and the Pöschl-Teller model initially at zero temperature. For the latter, we derive an analytical expression of the QNEC post-quench and numerically verify that the bound is again tight. Our study reinforces the validity of the QNEC as a bound on irreversible entropy production across various scenarios and highlights its optimization by models characterizing the most permissive bound on the second law. This suggests that the QNEC serves as a robust tool for analyzing quenches that influence both the initial state and the boundary conditions of quantum many-body systems under external sources.

quantum computing. To bring this technology to practical viability, it is essential to detect and mitigate material defects that cause decoherence. In this study, we employ terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy (SNOM) to examine the dielectric characteristics and defect-induced losses inherent in aluminum quantum circuit fabrics. By employing time-domain SNOM, we measure the complex permittivity of various components, including junctions, strays capacitors, and substrate surface features. Utilizing a fitted model, we derive the density of two-level systems (TLS) associated with aluminum-junction interfaces and interfaces between silicon dioxide (SiO$_2$) and silicon (Si) substrates. Our findings indicate that, under specific conditions, these al-junction interface TLS contribute significantly to loss. Furthermore, we report a previously unobserved density of substrate SiO$_2$ TLS ranging from $1\times 10^{18}$ to $1\times 10^{19} \, \text{cm}^{-3}$ within the bulk, located in the approximately 10 nm region adjacent to the SiO$_2$-Si interface. Collectively, these results offer both qualitative and quantitative evidence of where losses and defects originate within the device. Ultimately, our approach demonstrates a scalable method for rapidly characterizing and pinpointing the sources of losses in superconducting quantum computers.

The processes that formed and evolved Venus's atmosphere to its current surface conditions remain subjects of intense debate, encompassing questions that span multiple disciplines. We investigate these interconnected mechanisms, beginning with volatile sources and sinks, and trace the path from the deep interior to the upper atmosphere, covering volcanic outgassing, surface-atmosphere interactions, and atmospheric escape. Additionally, we address complex historical factors, such as the impact of Late Accretion events, the connection between magnetic field generation and long-term evolution, and the effects of geochemical and geodynamical feedback cycles on the atmosphere. Based on modeling and observations, we outline plausible evolutionary pathways for Venus from accretion to its present state. Three specific scenarios are highlighted: first, desiccation caused by atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase; second, a prolonged period of surface liquid water followed by climate destabilization and a runaway greenhouse effect; and third, inefficient outgassing that retained water within the planet, trapping hydrogen in the core and oxidizing the mantle. Finally, we discuss current evidence and the future observations and missions needed to refine our understanding of Venus's history and the intricate feedback cycles operating among its interior, surface, and atmosphere across past, present, and future timescales.

Among these, the Hawkes process is particularly popular due to its ability to define the probability of new events based on the process's history. This study focuses on the nonlinear Hawkes process, which effectively captures excitation and inhibition dynamics between different dimensions. Within a nonparametric Bayesian estimation framework, we derive concentration rates for the posterior distribution regarding the parameters, assuming only mild conditions on the prior and the model. These findings also establish convergence rates for Bayesian estimators. Additionally, a key aspect of event-data modeling is reconstructing the interaction graph, or Granger connectivity graph. We demonstrate consistency guarantees for Bayesian approaches in estimating the true interaction structure, specifically showing that the posterior distribution remains consistent for the process's parameters at a rate of $n^{-1/2}$ and that the Bayesian estimator for the Granger connectivity matrix achieves consistency under an edge-weighted adjacency matrix representation. Under a binary representation, consistency holds if a minimal number of edges exist (both excitatory and inhibitory) and these can be correctly oriented. Our proofs rely on novel techniques, such as bounding the Sobolev norm of the likelihood and employing local linearization methods. The proposed results enhance upon previous work by Baibouridou and Giannitsarou (2022). To illustrate these findings, we provide an application to a dataset consisting of earthquake magnitudes.

We introduce a plasma waveplate utilizing magneto-optical birefringence under a transverse magnetic field, designed to operate under ultra-high laser intensities. Uniquely, this device not only modifies the polarization state but also amplifies peak laser power. Numerical simulations demonstrate that a centimeter-scale waveplate can convert an initially linearly polarized pulse with 5 petawatts (PW) of peak power into a circularly polarized one with approximately 10 PW, achieving around 50% energy conversion efficiency. The proposed design parameters are compatible with current technology, and the proposed application effectively serves as a compact, high-power circular polarizer or a power-amplifying waveplate. This innovation facilitates the deployment of multi-petawatt lasers, which are essential for generating compact particle accelerators, emitting fundamental harmonic radiation in the exa-electronvolt range, and producing bright, coherent X-ray plasma sources via XUV harmonic generation. To achieve this, however, further advancements in high-power laser technology and plasma optical components are necessary. The late-time behavior of the SN~2020jfo across UV, optical, IR, and radio spectra aligns well with an expanding and cooling merger remnant, suggesting an approximately 0.5 solar mass ejecta envelope composed of heavy ions from r-process nucleosynthesis. Notably, the gamma-ray afterglow followed a single power-law evolution without a distinct break, indicating an unmagnetized fluid expanding in a medium with densities comparable to other detected cases. Ultimately, SN~2020jfo comprehensively displays all expected traits of a typical and luminous post-merger supernova, providing crucial insights into the dynamics and nucleosynthesis of the expanding ejecta, the early evolution of the kilonova, and the afterglow phases following the collision of two neutron stars. SN~2020jfo will serve as an ideal target for analyzing the connection between gravitational wave signals and electromagnetic emissions, as well as for r-process nucleosynthesis studies during the LIGO-Virgo observing run O4 and subsequent future campaigns.

Designed with quasi-static evolutionary applications in mind, our method utilizes a custom-developed Lagrangian formulation. Unlike traditional Eulerian approaches, this formulation calculates evolutionary evolution by comparing the configurations of specific stellar fluid elements at two consecutive time steps. Distinct from conventional variational principles, we independently vary the spatial coordinates of the fluid elements without constraining the displacement vector to be small, yielding Euler-Lagrange equations that differ significantly from the standard Hamiltonian energy variational principle. To solve these equations, we employ a new finite-element-like technique, which has been validated through application to both Newtonian and relativistic stars. Validation for general relativistic stars confirms that our method accurately determines the Hamiltonian energy via the energy variational principle. Furthermore, the final Hamiltonian energy is not constrained to match the initial value, allowing the star to reach a new equilibrium state. The method's significant advantage lies in its ability to minimize the Hamiltonian energy without imposing small-displacement constraints, a feature not found in conventional perturbation techniques. Although computationally more intensive than standard methods, the algorithm is parallelizable and, once optimized, will enable the evolutionary simulation of complex stellar systems, such as accreting neutron stars. Key original contributions include the development of the Lagrangian formulation and the finite-element-like solving technique for the resulting equations. Validation was conducted using the code ROXOS. The proposed approach is particularly well-suited for determining stationary states and can be extended to evolve systems over time. It may also be applicable to other fields, such as finding equilibrium configurations in molecular dynamics or continuum mechanics.

However, pandemic-related mobility restrictions drastically curtailed these urban encounters, prompting inquiries into their broader societal consequences. This study examines the long-term impacts of pandemic-induced mobility reductions on urban encounters and trust within European communities. Using a cross-national survey of 50,000 individuals across 22 European countries, we analyzed how shifts in the frequency of urban encounters and self-reported trust in strangers evolved between pre-pandemic conditions and the initial 12 months of lockdowns, with analyses stratified by the intensity of mobility constraints. Our findings indicate that reductions in urban encounters were substantial and, in several countries, unlikely to reverse within a year. Specifically, encounters with strangers declined by 25% to 40% in heavily locked-down areas, while overall urban encounters dropped by 15% to 25% in countries experiencing strict mobility restrictions. Furthermore, trust in strangers decreased significantly in countries with the toughest mobility limits (a 6% reduction) and increased mobility awareness (an 8% decline). These results highlight a potential contraction in the capacity for urban dwellers to leverage diverse interactions for innovation and social capital accumulation following the pandemic. Consequently, post-pandemic urban planning and policy must consciously prioritize the preservation and facilitation of physical encounters and social cohesion. By applying Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, we simulate the evolution of these fields to determine the Gaussian curvature of the parametric space, examining its behavior across phase transitions. In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "testing magnet"—via the Meissner effect. The resulting magnetic field gradient near the superconductor generates a centripetal acceleration on the atoms within the interferometer, enabling detection through atomic interference patterns. Building on the fact that gravitational acceleration of atoms has been measured with a precision of $10^{-12}$ g, the sensitivity of this method for detecting the expelled local field could potentially achieve $10^{-14}$ T. Our proposed apparatus comprises three main sections: an experimental region, a shielding region containing the superconductor, and a preparation region. To enable the use of larger-area high-temperature superconducting disks and account for magnetic fields arising from current guides on the disk's surface, we implemented a complex coil arrangement in our design. Additionally, to prevent contamination from ambient magnetic fields, we employed a configuration utilizing three orthogonal shieldings, each with a distinct orientation relative to the atomic interferometer arms. Although this setup is complex, it offers the advantage of being free from end-field effects that typically limit the sensitivity of standard solenoid measurements. We also discuss potential extensions, including the application of this sensing technique to tiny grains of high-temperature superconductors, samples exhibiting the Mössbauer effect, and neutral atoms subjected to the Stark effect. Ultimately, we aim to demonstrate that the proposed arrangement can detect the Meissner effect in a high-temperature superconducting disk while achieving a sensitivity of $10^{-14}$ T at the location of the atomic interferometer. We have identified a broad category of object-oriented programs, including many significant real-world applications, that can be efficiently executed on massively parallel SIMD accelerators. We term this category Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), as it expresses parallelism by executing a specific method across all instances of a given type.

To enable average programmers to utilize fast GPU programming for SMMO applications, we developed DynaSOAr, a CUDA framework. DynaSOAr comprises three core components: (1) a fully parallel, lock-free, dynamic memory allocator; (2) a data layout Domain-Specific Language (DSL); and (3) an efficient, parallel do-all operation. By controlling both memory allocation and access, DynaSOAr outperforms state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators.

DynaSOAr enhances memory utilization by adopting a Structure of Arrays (SoA) data layout and reduces memory fragmentation through the efficient management of free and allocated blocks using lock-free, hierarchical bitmaps. Unlike other allocators, our design relies heavily on atomic operations, prioritizing overall application performance over minimal per-thread allocation/deallocation overhead.

To maximize memory access throughput, DynaSOAr's data layout DSL distributes the memory of each object instance contiguously and aligns memories of objects within the same thread block (containing up to 512 threads in current CUDA versions) in a coalesced manner. This results in a performance penalty that scales with the number of object instances rather than the volume of data per instance, making the DSL highly effective for large-record, multiple-object problems.

Furthermore, DynaSOAr represents the do-all operation using a hierarchical, tree-based structure, minimizing global synchronization points and maximizing parallel execution. By employing these three strategies, DynaSOAr achieves near-ideal occupancy and bandwidth utilization for single-method multiple-object problems on current GPU architectures.

Evaluations on real-world applications and synthetic benchmarks using various object types and data sizes on the NVIDIA Tesla K40 demonstrate that DynaSOAr achieves a 2x to 8x speedup over current hand-written CUDA alternatives for Darcy flow simulation and molecular dynamics.

This paper addresses the question of determining the maximum value of $\lambda$ such that any 2-edge-coloring of the complete graph on $\mathbb{N}$ guarantees a monochromatic infinite $F$-factor with a vertex set possessing an upper density of at least $\lambda$, for a given finite graph $F$. We establish a novel lower bound for this problem; for specific graphs $F$, including cliques and odd cycles, this bound is optimal as it aligns with a previously known upper bound. Furthermore, in the specific instance where $F$ is a triangle, we provide an explicit lower bound of $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}} \approx 0.62203$, which surpasses the earlier best result of $3/5$. Along the way, we demonstrate that for any graph $F$ for which the minimum degree $\delta(F)$ exceeds half the number of vertices $|V(F)|$, the lower bound derived by Erdős and Galvin is optimal. Additionally, we introduce a generalized Ramsey problem involving a parameter $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and explore connections to a corresponding fractional issue. Our findings generalize the work of Montellano-Ballesteros and Rosales. Our approach relies on constructing specific graphs with large independent sets utilizing a dynamical systems framework, as developed by Bergelson and McCutcheon. We also analyze several sub-optimal lower bounds found in existing literature, comparing them with our results.

This study utilizes QED particle-in-cell simulations that incorporate electron-positron spin and photon polarization to examine a standard laser-solid configuration where an ultraintense linearly polarized laser strikes a foil target featuring a micrometer-scale preplasma. Our results indicate that when laser intensity surpasses $10^{23}~\rm W/\rm cm^2$ and positron yield becomes significant, the produced positrons exhibit clear polarization. Specifically, these polarized positrons can achieve a polarization degree exceeding 30% and a charge greater than 30 nC, with a flux of $10^{12}\,\rm s^{-1}$. The degree of polarization varies with deflection angle, reaching up to 60% at 3 mrad. This angular dependence arises from laser field self-compression within the plasma, which generates a localized, extremely strong, and linearly polarized QED vacuum current carrying electron charge. This current attracts positrons primarily from the front of the laser pulse, imparting distinct spin orientation. Furthermore, this mechanism is robust and can achieve even higher polarization levels with future lasers. Additionally, another method to increase polarization is suggested by optimizing parameters relative to the laser wavelength. This positron source offers significant potential for advancing fundamental spin physics, investigating QED effects, and developing beam-matter interaction techniques, particularly for enhancing laser-driven gamma-ray photon and gamma-ray laser production.

In this work, assuming $|S|$ is bounded, we identify groups with polynomial diameter as those possessing a substantial abelian section near the top, specifically one whose size constitutes an exponential fraction of the total group order. This finding extends a significant result by Breuillard and Tointon. Consequently, groups exhibiting polynomial diameter are shown to contain a large nilpotent subgroup of class at most $2$ and to possess a high number of conjugacy classes. These results generalize a theorem by *Breuillard* and one by *L^e* and *Wall*. Furthermore, we establish a polynomial bound for the diameter of groups constrained by a fixed number of conjugacy classes and size. This improves upon a theorem by *L^e* and, under the assumption that the degree of the polynomials is also bounded, allows us to show such groups have polynomial diameter, thereby refining a result by *Breuillard*, *Sarnak*, and *Tointon*. Along the way, we provide a new characterization of groups with polynomial number of conjugacy classes in terms of the Lie-Kolca condition. If $G$ is simple and possesses a large abelian section, then it too has polynomial diameter; this extends a theorem by *Guralnick* and *Saxl*. An analogous result holds for almost simple groups.

We analyze both inextensible and highly extensible membranes, detailing the influence of membrane tension in each scenario. When the inner fluid is denser than the outer fluid, both systems display a centrifugally induced Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability that competes with restoring forces from curvature and tension, ultimately determining the finger scale. Numerical continuation methods are employed to calculate strongly nonlinear primary finger states up to self-contact, as well as secondary branches involving mixed modes and circumferentially localized folds, varying with rotation rate and external pressure. The analysis includes both reflection-symmetric and symmetry-broken chiral configurations, with results illustrated through bifurcation diagrams. Furthermore, the ratio of the system scale to the natural length scale is identified as the key factor governing the sequence of primary bifurcations from the unperturbed circular state, as well as the resulting solution profiles and the initiation of secondary bifurcations. The differences in finger profiles and bifurcation behaviors between the two membranes are attributed to the distribution of external pressure and the balance between internal and external forces. These findings offer insights into the nonlinear dynamics of the instability and how it is regulated by the system's geometric and physical parameters, addressing a scenario relevant to the protoplanetary disk instability in nature. The governing physical process involves the centrifugally driven Rayleigh-Taylor instability of the heavier inner fluid, countered by the membrane's curvature and tension forces. This process is influenced by external pressure and the cell's geometry, which set the ratio of the system's natural length scale to its size. The primary bifurcation from the circular state is reflection symmetric, yet secondary bifurcations produce chiral folds, resulting in a symmetry-breaking phenomenon reminiscent of the Sagnac effect. While the primary instability is directly analogous to Rayleigh-Taylor instability under external acceleration, the overall problem introduces complexities due to the domain's curvature and the balance of external, internal, and external forces. These factors cause significant deviations from the standard Hele-Shaw dynamics, causing the system to operate across a broad spectrum of intermediate to high capillary and inertial regimes. The model assumes external pressure distribution and membrane material properties that are both rotationally symmetric and time-independent. Although the setup is inherently inertial, we account for the balance of all external forces, including those arising from external pressure, while also considering the possible slip of the membrane at the contact line with the cell wall. Machine translation evaluation has advanced from simple word-overlap metrics like BLEU to more sophisticated string-based methods such as rule-based and model-based approaches. These newer techniques assess translations by analyzing linguistic properties, leveraging the assumption that better translations score higher across various language dimensions. This study examines these language property correlations using a statistical framework, investigating a broad range of properties for both source and target languages, including syntax, semantics, and specific linguistic aspects relevant to machine translation. Our analysis of English-to-German and Chinese-to-English pairs reveals that while semantic property correlations correlate well with translation quality, other property types show only marginal improvements over random guesses. Furthermore, we identify that the benefit of any single property type is often mediated by others, and we highlight common data issues affecting the interpreted results. Ultimately, our findings suggest that current translating models may underutilize certain language properties and that the performance of semantic evaluation metrics can be enhanced by a diverse set of source language properties.

Utilizing low-energy effective field theories (EFTs) to model general neutrino interactions and Dirac fermion DM coupled to charm quarks, we conduct an analysis of recent LHCb data. Furthermore, we propose a specific photon-neutrino-neutrino interaction that could enhance the DM signal in future direct detection experiments, an effect also observable through final states in associated production. This enhancement is generated by a dimension-six EFT operator, which we analyze as it connects to heavier physics, such as lepton flavor violation and light supersymmetric DM. We also highlight the potential of upcoming dedicated searches at the Jefferson Lab 12 GeV upgrade and the Fermilab Hubbell Hall neutron facility. We conclude by suggesting a target asymmetry of ${\cal O}(10^{-9})$ for a future muon $g-2$ experiment, which would push the exclusion curve closer to the region allowed by the $g-2$ anomaly. —defined as the likelihood that the fraction of time up to $t$ during which a random walk $S$ with i.i.d. zero-mean increments (taking finitely many values) remains non-negative exceeds $x$ for all $s \in [1,t]$—decays according to the power law $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b)/2}$. Introduction

Localizing visible sound sources in video is a fundamental task with wide-ranging applications, including video editing, forensic analysis, and human-computer interaction. Although numerous datasets exist for this purpose, most entries consist of multiple annotations per image, making it difficult for readers to precisely locate where specific sounds originate. To address this challenge, we aim to localize visible sound sources accurately.

This allows us to overcome limitations imposed by traditional visual feature cues, such as those found in occluded, blurry, or heavily cropped objects. significant recent interest. While most GCNs operate within the nonlinear domain, conducting graph convolutions in the linear domain has historically been computationally expensive and complex. This paper introduces the linear graph convolutional network (LGCN), which performs all operations in the linear domain to ensure computational efficiency. We demonstrate that a standard graph convolutional layer can be elevated to a linear operation by utilizing the degree matrix as a weight matrix. To ensure backward compatibility, we propose calculating the degree matrix dynamically based on node features rather than the graph structure itself; this allows us to use a static degree matrix for graphs that remain unchanged over time. Empirical results on three sentiment analysis and one node classification tasks indicate that LGCN achieves comparable performance to recent GCN methods while reducing training time, training data preprocessing time, and inference time by approximately 50%. For networks comprising layers that do not change, the total training time can be reduced to one quarter of that of existing methods. Additionally, we show that LGCN achieves the same performance for a hand-written graph SAGE layer, confirming the general applicability of our approach. Graph self-supervised learning (GSSL) has emerged as a promising solution, enhancing model quality through various pretraining strategies. However, current GSSL methods are limited by the assumption of a fixed graph structure, as changing the structure incurs high computational costs. Although recent attempts to improve this still rely on expensive nonlinear graph convolutional layers, our evaluations show that these methods remain 10 times slower than traditional GCNs. This slowness stems from the necessity to compute and store a dense matrix representing all possible edge combinations. To overcome these limitations, we introduce GSSL-V (Graph Self-supervised Learning with Vector Representation), the first GSSL framework to achieve comparable performance gains over state-of-the-art methods with a 10-fold reduction in time complexity. Like prior art, GSSL-V (unlike other approaches) uses vector representations to encode structural information, enabling the model to capture topological data without calculating and storing a dense matrix. Our evaluations on three GSSL tasks show that GSSL-V matches the performance of state-of-the-art methods while being 10 times faster, and it also outperforms graph few-shot learning methods. Upon implementing this condition via the standard Faddeev-Popov procedure, the resulting gauge-fixed action retains a dependence on a single gauge parameter. This indicates that the harmonic gauge represents a family of conditions rather than a unique one. This perspective provides a physical justification for covariant harmonic gauges, which arise when a mass term is introduced for the gravitational perturbation. Specifically, selecting a particular harmonic gauge yields a theory of linearized massive gravity with the expected five degrees of freedom, successfully avoiding the vDVZ discontinuity that plagues the standard Fierz-Pauli theory. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a Dirac-Brauer type mass term yields identical results. Importantly, this equivalence between the two approaches to linearized massive gravity is non-trivial, as it depends on gauge transformations that involve derivatives of the mass parameter. These derivations are performed in the flat Minkowski background. The findings are subsequently generalized to curved spacetimes, where the analysis encompasses the full non-linear theory, confirming that the proposed harmonic gauges remain valid beyond the linear approximation. The degree of masslessness achieved by these gauges varies with the curvature scalar, ensuring that the number of propagating degrees of freedom remains consistently at five. We contend that this degree of masslessness is optimal, as it aligns with the expectations for a fundamental theory describing massive gravity in an expanding universe. Finally, we outline potential applications, including an alternative formulation of bigravity and a framework for linearized gauge invariant perturbation theory.

Introduction {#s-intro}
============

The notion of negative absolute temperature often generates intrigue and excitement, yet it can also lead to confusion and skepticism, particularly when introducing the topic to undergraduates. While we are not claiming that negative temperature introduces a fundamental flaw in the laws of physics or thermodynamics, the phenomenon can appear somewhat artificial, akin to exploiting loopholes, tricks, or loopholes in physical principles. Despite this potential for unease, negative temperature is undeniably real and has been experimentally verified multiple times.

In this brief note, we utilize a straightforward model—the system of two energy levels—to demonstrate that negative temperature is indeed authentic. Although the full details involving statistical mechanics, Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions, and the specific heat curve are beyond the scope of this note, we use the two-level system to show that concepts associated with negative temperature are real, tangible, and verifiable. Our approach includes calculations from both statistical mechanics and thermodynamics perspectives, alongside explanations that address potential misconceptions. We contend that the term "negative absolute zero" is oxymoronic and misleading; even negative temperature does not imply falsehood, as the word "absolute" suggests. Although achieving negative temperature is challenging, it is not impossible.

Recent experimental demonstrations have confirmed that negative temperature is a genuine physical state. By extending the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw with the minimal dark sector, we establish a physical mechanism for neutrino oscillation lengths: the atmospheric mass scale originates from tree-level seesaw dynamics, whereas the solar scale emerges radiatively through mediation by the dark sector. We pinpoint parameter regions that satisfy theoretical constraints, align with dark matter relic density, and are viable under direct detection limits. Employing two-loop renormalization group equations, we investigate vacuum stability and the consistency of the fundamental dark parity symmetry, while also deriving a lower bound for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. We establish that a coherent missing momentum scale of approximately 10 TeV is necessitated by current data, and we outline potential future constraints arising from neutrino coherence. Additionally, we analyze the model's behavior at the linear collider scale using effective field theory. Regarding the dominant contribution to the $W$ boson mass, we demonstrate that certain configurations can account for the anomalous result reported by the LHCb collaboration. Finally, we detail the characteristic signatures of this framework at the future Circular Lepton Collider. Abstract: We examine the consistency of electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino oscillation mechanisms, and dark matter relic density in the minimal scoto-seesaw model. By establishing a structured approach to neutrino oscillation scales, we identify parameter spaces compatible with vacuum stability, the neutrinoless double beta decay limit, and direct dark matter detection bounds. We derive a lower bound for the coherent missing momentum scale of roughly 10 TeV and discuss its implications for interpreting the $W$ boson mass anomaly at the LHC. We also specify the model's effective field theory behavior at the linear collider scale and detail its signature at the future Circular Lepton Collider.

Specifically, for toric complete intersections containing simple normal crossings divisors that include the indeterminacy loci, we demonstrate that the corresponding relative $I$-functions are equivalent. In the case of toric complete intersections with smooth divisors, we establish that the corresponding relative $I$-functions are equivalent up to an exponential factor. These findings were previously addressed by You for complete intersections and by Chen for simple normal crossings divisors. Our approach relies on the equivalence between Fan--Wu--You's mirror symmetry and the Gromov--Witten/longitudinal Landau-Ginburg correspondence established by Ellen--Katz--Peyvanestamati. Furthermore, we explore implications regarding the equivalence of relative quantum cohomology under birational transformations. If our demonstrations regarding simple normal crossings and smooth divisors are correct, then the corresponding relative quantum cohomologies are indeed equivalent, as the birational flips connecting our constructed divisors are crepant. Consequently, our results align with the predictions of Bryan--Galkin--Jorgenson--Kontsevich--Peyvanestamati--Shou--You and the findings of [KW]. Moreover, our exponential factor correction completes the arguments of [KW] and [EL-KP]. Additionally, we provide a constructive method for determining the specific form of this factor, which varies from the results in [EL-KP] and [KW]. These methods are illustrated through examples involving toric del Pezzo surfaces and threefold complete intersections. A key component of our proof is the utilization of mutation equations, a concept introduced by Bryan--Galkin--Jorgenson--Kontsevich and further developed by Peyvanestamati and us. Additionally, we establish a direct derivation of the mirror theorem for simple normal crossings divisors via mutation equations and demonstrate that the differential isomorphism between longitudinal theories under birational transformations yields the equivalence of their quantum cohomologies.

The tool incorporates various statistical techniques, including standard and weighted Principal Component Analysis (PCA), elastic maps (a non-linear PCA variant), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), multilinear regression, K-Means clustering, and a decision tree algorithm variant. Featuring intuitive interfaces for customizing data point attributes (size, shape, color) and a rapid 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables users to build interactive 3D scenes representing data points and their relationships. This decision tree algorithm, which operates without predefined classes, utilizes a "scissoring plane" method in high-dimensional space to sever links between unrelated points while preserving those among related ones; the resulting 3D tree structure can be extracted via standard tree extraction techniques. Furthermore, the system supports the integration of existing 3D models (such as characters or vehicles) to represent specific data points.
